Harness Engineering · Applied Lens · Snapshot: September 2026 🌐

Harness Engineering Across Real-World Contexts: One Pattern, Nine Domains

The same agent harness — context, model, planning loop, tools, state, verification, approvals, action — now runs code reviews, contact centres, sales pipelines, legal review, procurement, hospital operations, construction projects, factories and research teams. What changes from one domain to the next is not the loop but its parts: where context comes from, which tools the agent may touch, how its work is checked, and when a human must say yes. This visual guide walks the universal pattern, nine domain adaptations, real incidents that show what a missing layer costs, the regulation that now requires some layers, and a runnable model of how much autonomy each domain can afford.

How to read this: an applied companion to the research, production, market and case-study lenses. Domain descriptions are architectural patterns, not endorsements of particular products. Incidents and regulations are linked in References. The autonomy simulator uses stated, illustrative assumptions — change them to fit your own case.
01The universal harness pattern 02Building blocks & the harness "equation" 03Nine domains, one loop 04How the harness changes by context 05How much autonomy can a domain afford? 06Real incidents: the missing layer 07Where regulation requires layers 08Adoption sweet spots 09Design principles checklist

01 The Universal Harness Pattern

Strip away the domain vocabulary and every production agent follows nine stages. A request arrives; the harness assembles context; the model reasons; a planning loop breaks the job into steps and picks tools; tools act on external systems; the harness observes results and handles errors; durable state records what happened; verification and approvals check the work; and only then does a final action or answer leave the system. Stages 4–7 repeat until the plan is done. Press play to follow one task through — then switch domain to see the same stages with different contents:

▶ One task through the nine stages Same loop, domain-specific contents.

Two properties make this pattern reusable. First, the model is the only part that is general-purpose; everything around it — the connectors, the tool permissions, the checks, the approval rules — encodes domain knowledge. Second, the loop is closed by observation: an agent that cannot see the result of its own action (a failing test, a rejected API call, an out-of-range sensor reading) cannot correct itself, whatever the domain.

02 Core Building Blocks and the Harness "Equation"

The nine stages are built from eight reusable blocks. A popular way to summarise it is an equation: Model + Context + Tools + State + Governance + Verification = Domain Harness. The equation is a useful checklist but a misleading formula: the blocks don't add, they multiply. A harness with a superb model and no verification isn't 85% safe — it's as weak as its missing layer. Switch blocks off to see which failures become possible:

▶ Remove a block, see what breaks Click blocks to toggle.
BlockWhat it providesTypical implementation
Model intelligenceLanguage, reasoning, planningFrontier or domain-tuned LLM; routing between cheap and strong models
Domain context / retrievalThe facts the model doesn't knowRAG over documents, database queries, code indexes, knowledge graphs
Tools / APIsThe ability to actFunction calling, MCP servers, scripted actions, RPA
Durable state & memoryContinuity across steps, sessions, crashesSession stores, checkpoints, durable workflows, artifact storage
Policies, permissions & guardrailsWhat the agent may and may not doScoped credentials, allow-lists, input/output filters, rate and spend limits
Verification / evaluationEvidence the work is rightTests, citation checks, rule engines, simulations, LLM judges, evals
Human-in-the-loopAccountability for consequential actionsApproval queues, escalation, take-over, sign-off
Observability / loggingThe ability to audit and improveTraces, metrics, audit logs, replay

03 Nine Domains, One Loop

Each domain plugs its own sources, tools and checks into the same loop. Pick a domain to see its flow — sources on the left, the agent's actions in the middle, the output and its gate on the right — plus what the harness has to change and a real-world anchor:

▶ Domain explorer Sources → agent → actions → gated output

Read across the nine and a pattern appears. Context sources go from text-heavy (code, tickets, contracts) to structured and physical (ERP ledgers, EHR records, BIM models, SCADA telemetry). Verification goes from mechanical and cheap (unit tests, schema checks) to expert and expensive (clinical review, engineering sign-off). And the final action goes from easily reversible (a pull request nobody merged) to irreversible (a payment sent, a medication scheduled, a valve opened). The further right a domain sits on those three axes, the more of the harness is about control rather than capability.

04 How the Harness Changes by Context

The same six dimensions, compared across six representative domains. Hover a cell for detail; the colour shows how demanding that dimension is:

▶ Harness requirements matrix Darker = more demanding
Hover a cell.

One nuance the matrix hides: risk belongs to actions, not domains. A software agent that edits code in a branch is low-risk; the same agent running DROP TABLE against production is not (see the Replit incident below). A customer-service agent answering "where is my parcel?" is low-risk; the same agent promising a refund creates a binding commitment (see Air Canada). Good harnesses therefore tier approvals by action within a domain, not only by domain.

05 How Much Autonomy Can a Domain Afford?

Every harness picks a point between "the agent just acts" and "a human approves everything". The right point depends on four numbers: how often the agent is wrong, how many of those errors automated checks catch, what an error that escapes costs, and how long a human takes to review. Pick a preset or move the sliders; the chart shows expected cost per 1,000 tasks for four policies:

▶ Autonomy policy simulator Illustrative assumptions — same formulas as the script below.
"""Same harness, different domains: which level of autonomy is cheapest?

For each domain we model 1,000 agent tasks and compare four harness policies:
  auto    - agent acts directly, no checks
  verify  - automated verification (tests, citation check, rules, simulation) catches a share of errors
  human   - automated verification, then a human approves every task
  tiered  - automated verification; a human approves only the riskiest 20% of tasks,
            which (by assumption) hold 80% of the potential damage
Expected cost = errors that escape x cost per error + human review minutes x $2/min.
All numbers are illustrative assumptions, not measurements. Standard library only.
"""
N, HUMAN_CATCH, RATE, TIER_SHARE, TIER_RISK = 1000, 0.90, 2.0, 0.20, 0.80

#          domain               error  auto-check  $ per escaped  review
#                               rate   catches     error          minutes
DOMAINS = [("Software",          0.15, 0.70,          50,          8),
           ("Customer service",  0.05, 0.30,          30,          3),
           ("Sales / RevOps",    0.08, 0.20,          20,          2),
           ("Research",          0.12, 0.50,         200,         12),
           ("Finance",           0.04, 0.80,        2000,          5),
           ("AEC / construction",0.10, 0.40,        5000,         15),
           ("Legal",             0.10, 0.50,       20000,         25),
           ("Healthcare ops",    0.06, 0.40,       50000,          6),
           ("Industrial",        0.05, 0.60,      100000,         10)]

def costs(err, check, dollars, minutes):
    after_check = err * (1 - check)
    auto = N * err * dollars
    verify = N * after_check * dollars
    human = N * after_check * (1 - HUMAN_CATCH) * dollars + N * minutes * RATE
    tiered = (N * after_check * (TIER_RISK * (1 - HUMAN_CATCH) + (1 - TIER_RISK)) * dollars
              + N * TIER_SHARE * minutes * RATE)
    return {"auto": auto, "verify": verify, "human": human, "tiered": tiered}

print(f"Expected cost per {N:,} tasks (errors that escape + human time)\n")
print(f"{'domain':<20}{'auto':>12}{'verify':>12}{'human':>12}{'tiered':>12}   best")
for name, *p in DOMAINS:
    c = costs(*p)
    best = min(c, key=c.get)
    print(f"{name:<20}" + "".join(f"{'$' + format(round(v), ','):>12}" for v in c.values()) + f"   {best}")
print("\nSame harness, same policies: cheap mistakes favour automated checks alone; mid-cost ones a risk-tiered\nhuman gate; expensive, hard-to-reverse ones a human on every action.")

Output:

Expected cost per 1,000 tasks (errors that escape + human time)

domain                      auto      verify       human      tiered   best
Software                  $7,500      $2,250     $16,225      $3,830   verify
Customer service          $1,500      $1,050      $6,105      $1,494   verify
Sales / RevOps            $1,600      $1,280      $4,128      $1,158   tiered
Research                 $24,000     $12,000     $25,200      $8,160   tiered
Finance                  $80,000     $16,000     $11,600      $6,480   tiered
AEC / construction      $500,000    $300,000     $60,000     $90,000   human
Legal                 $2,000,000  $1,000,000    $150,000    $290,000   human
Healthcare ops        $3,000,000  $1,800,000    $192,000    $506,400   human
Industrial            $5,000,000  $2,000,000    $220,000    $564,000   human

Same harness, same policies: cheap mistakes favour automated checks alone; mid-cost ones a risk-tiered
human gate; expensive, hard-to-reverse ones a human on every action.

Three lessons fall out of the numbers. Automated verification is almost always worth it: it beats "auto" in every row because it costs no human time. A human on every action only pays when errors are expensive — in software and customer service it multiplies cost several-fold. And risk tiering is the middle ground: sending only the riskiest fifth of tasks to a human wins in sales, research and finance. The crossover moves with the cost per error, which is why the same harness ships with different approval rules per domain. (The model ignores reputational and legal costs that don't scale linearly — the reason regulated domains keep humans in the loop even when the arithmetic is close.)

07 Where Regulation Requires Layers

In several domains the human-in-the-loop, logging and verification blocks are no longer optional design choices:

RuleScopeHarness layers it requires
EU AI Act, Article 14 (human oversight)High-risk AI systems (e.g. employment, credit, essential services, critical infrastructure)Interfaces that let people monitor, interpret, override and stop the system; trained overseers. Stand-alone high-risk obligations apply from 2 Dec 2027 and product-embedded ones from 2 Aug 2028, after the Digital Omnibus (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744) deferred the original 2 Aug 2026 date.
EU AI Act, Article 12 (record-keeping)High-risk AI systemsAutomatic event logs over the system's lifetime — the observability block.
HIPAA "minimum necessary" standardUS protected health informationScoped retrieval and permissions: the agent should see only the PHI a task needs.
Court and bar rules on AI-drafted filingsLegal practice (many courts, after Mata v. Avianca)Citation verification and a lawyer's sign-off on every filing.
Consumer-protection liabilityCustomer-facing statements (Moffatt v. Air Canada)Policy-grounded answers and approval for commitments: the company is bound by what its bot says.

Harness engineering across contexts in one paragraph
A general-purpose model becomes a domain-specific worker through its harness. The loop — context, reason, plan, act, observe, remember, verify, approve, act — is the same in a repository, a contact centre, a law firm, a hospital and a factory. What changes is the plumbing (which systems feed context and accept actions), the checks (tests and schemas where errors are cheap, experts and simulations where they are not) and the approval rules (tiered by the cost and reversibility of each action, and increasingly set by regulation). Adoption follows that cost curve: software, service and sales first, professional domains next, physical and safety-critical domains last. The model may be shared; the harness is where the domain lives.

⚠️ Notes

Corrections and additions to the source infographic: (1) the "Harness Equation" is additive but harnesses are not — a missing verification or permission block is not a small deduction but an open failure path, as the incidents in section 06 show; (2) risk is per action, not per domain — the infographic rates Software's human-approval need "Low–Medium" and Customer Service "Medium", yet the best-known harness failures (Replit deleting a production database; Air Canada bound by its chatbot's refund promise) came from exactly those domains, when a low-risk agent took a high-risk action; (3) regulation is missing — the EU AI Act makes human oversight (Art. 14) and logging (Art. 12) mandatory for high-risk systems, now from 2 December 2027 for stand-alone systems after the Digital Omnibus deferral, and HIPAA's minimum-necessary rule shapes healthcare retrieval; (4) the infographic presents adoption waves without evidence; we treat them as a reasonable ordering, not a measured result. The autonomy simulator's numbers are illustrative assumptions.
